seriesStmt.p: Machine readable texts of the unpublished correspondence of James Joyce

msIdentifier.repository: Beinecke Rare Book & Manuscript Library, Yale University

projectDesc.p: James Joyce's unpublished correspondence, collected, annotated, and made available as a digital edition

div.p: Many thanks for your article especially for your kind remembering of my voice. Those are the things we begin to like at our age. I sent you Bravo with a picture of Sullivan in the back ground and as you will see by the enclosed letter I am trying to work up Antheil to do Cain for him. What do you think about this? He asked me to suggest a subject for Opera. If you approve will you write to him about it.

If you have read in the paper that I was smashed up and hospitalled in a taxi collision here do not believe it. I got off very lightly considering, but I am still a little under the shock. My eyes were unhurt.

I hope all is going well with you in the best of all possible Rapallos
.

note.p: Pound’s article “Storicamente Joyce (e censura),” an historical survey of JJ’s career and struggles with censorship, was published, in Italian, in the Genoa journal L’Indice, vol. 1, no. 11 (September 1930): 3. The article combined Pound’s recent opinions with translated borrowings from his early articles on JJ, especially “‘Dubliners’ and Mr. James Joyce,” The Egoist, vol. 1, no. 14 (15 July 1914): 267. To clarify allusions that might baffle Italian readers, the editors of L’Indice inserted explanations at points in the article. Pound complained of these “note” in a postcard to JJ from Rapallo postmarked 15 September 1930: “These latins will SIMPLIFY what they think dont matter in most embarearsing manner” (Robert Spoo, “Unpublished Letters of Ezra Pound to James, Nora, and Stanislaus Joyce,” James Joyce Quarterly, vol. 32, no. 3-4 [Spring-Summer 1995]: 553).

In 1930-1931, Pound contributed more than a score of articles to L’Indice, many under the caption “Appunti” (“Notes”), on subjects ranging from Jean Cocteau to Leo Frobenius. A number of his own poems and prose writings (including How to Read) also appeared there in translation by various hands. On 8 April 1930, he wrote Wyndham Lewis that L’Indice “is most active fortnightly or other rev. in Italy” (Pound/Lewis: The Letters of Ezra Pound and Wyndham Lewis, ed. Timothy Materer [New York: New Directions, 1985], 170).

div.note: Pound wrote in “Storicamente Joyce (e censura)”: “Joyce ha una bellissima voce di tenore, guastata per poco uso. Nego l’effetto di questa voce sulla formazione dei suoi romanzi. … E’ vero che Joyce canta magnificamente (fra I suoi intimi) canti burleschi” (“Joyce has a most beautiful tenor voice, spoiled by little use. I deny the effect of this voice on the formation of his novels. … It’s true that Joyce sings comic songs magnificently [among his intimate friends]”) (L’Indice, vol. 1, no. 11 [September 1930]: 3).

Bravo, published in Paris by Jacques Théry (1881-1970) and André Lang (1893-1986), was a topical, photo-filled magazine that promised “tous les spectacles” and covered the contemporary scene in art, music, literature, and film, with an emphasis on celebrities and popular figures of the day. Photo clusters featured stylish men and women, aristocrats, and “vedettes” (leading men and ladies) of the stage and film. Talented writers, such as André Maurois, Paul Morand, Colette, and JJ’s friend Philippe Soupault (1897-1990), wrote lively articles for the periodical. Produced in a large format (11 x 14 inches) with bold, striking covers, and offering 40 or 50 pages per issue, Bravo began as a weekly in November 1929 but by September 1930 had become a monthly, selling for five francs.

note.p: The September 1930 number of Bravo contained an article by Philippe Soupault, “Autour de James Joyce” (“Around James Joyce”), Bravo: mensuel, no. 21 (September 1930): 16-17, in which Soupault declared himself “proud to be able to state that I have met in my life two men whose genius seemed dazzling to me. … Pablo Picasso and James Joyce. … The name of James Joyce bursts like a storm. In the Old and the New World he stirs up the most lively quarrels. All those who are for the paralyzing tradition, all those who fear everything that is new, strive to have it believed that ‘all of that (the work of Joyce!) is humbug,’ or again, ‘it is snobbery!’ But others who are more clear-sighted declare simply that this writer brings, at last, a brilliant light and frees literature from all the ridiculous bonds with which time, criticism, and professors had so constricted it that it was ready to suffocate and die” (16).

Despairing of capturing JJ’s genius in a single essay, Soupault states that, instead, he will “place around this impressive figure the atmosphere that surrounds him like a halo” (“placer autour de cette impressionante figure, l’atmosphère qui l’auréole”) (16). In this sense, Soupault will write not about JJ but “around” him (“Autour de James Joyce”). JJ’s present emotional surroundings include, notably, his campaign to obtain justice for the under-appreciated Irish tenor, John O’Sullivan, or Sullivan (1877-1955), a leading interpreter of the role of Arnold in the opera Guillaume Tell (1829) by the Italian composer Gioachino Rossini (1792-1868). Soupault tells of JJ’s attending a performance of Guillaume Tell at the Paris Opéra on a night when another tenor sang Arnold. “He was being applauded vigorously, and no one was noticing that this tenor was evading the important bits (“escamotait des fragments importants”) of the score of Guillaume Tell because he was incapable of singing them like Sullivan, one of the rare tenors who can sing this opera in its entirety. James Joyce could not contain his indignation, and he shouted out an insult at the skill of this tenor-conjurer (“ténor escamoteur”) and a cheer in honor of Sullivan” (17). (For other accounts of JJ’s bizarre behavior during his efforts to promote O’Sullivan, see Ellmann, JJ 624-27.)

Soupault’s article was accompanied by two photographs. One was a close-up of JJ’s face credited to “Martinie.” This image would appear to be one of several photographs of JJ produced circa 1925 by the Paris photographer of noted “personalities,” Henri Martinie, 19 rue de Penthièvre, who produced studio photographs also of Sylvia Beach, Adrienne Monnier, George Antheil, Robert McAlmon, and many French authors of the day. The other photograph, probably from 1929, showed JJ seated next to the Irish poet James Stephens (1880-1950), with “le ténor irlandais Sullivan” standing behind them. This latter photograph is the “picture of Sullivan in the back ground” that JJ mentions in the present letter to Pound. (This image is reproduced in Ellmann, JJ photograph page XLVI.) On 11 September 1930, while vacationing in the coastal French town of Étretat, JJ cabled Shakespeare and Company to have six copies of Bravo delivered to him (James Joyce’s Letters to Sylvia Beach, 1921-1940, ed. Melissa Banta and Oscar Silverman [Bloomington: Indiana University Press, 1987], 166). He was evidently distributing the Bravo number as part of his “Sullivanizing” campaign. (For a fuller account of JJ and O’Sullivan, see Lucia Joyce to Pound, 22 February 1930, notes.)

Sylvia Beach (1887-1962), the American expatriate bookstore owner and publisher of Ulysses in France, contributed an article to Bravo: “La campagne autant que Paris,” Bravo: le magazine moderne, no. 45 (October 1932): 18-19.

George Antheil (1900-1959), American avant-garde composer and self-styled “bad boy of music,” whom Pound met in Paris in 1923 and actively promoted, claiming that the young man “has made a beginning; that is in writing music that couldn’t have been written before. … There is edge. There is the use of the piano, no longer melodic, or cantabile, but solid, unified as one drum” (Pound, Antheil and the Treatise on Harmony [1924; rpt. New York: Da Capo Press, 1968], 62). Though he wrote more conventionally scored music, Antheil is best known for his Ballet Mécanique, which premiered in Paris in June 1926 with a cacophonous instrumentation that included eight pianos and two airplane propellers. Pound reported a crowded, boisterous theater: “People sitting on strapontins [folding-seats]. Landslide pro Antheil” (Ezra Pound to His Parents: Letters 1895-1929, ed. Mary de Rachewiltz et al. [Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2010], 600). JJ attended a private performance of the piece, “a part of which he said was like Mozart” (Ellmann, JJ 557).

Antheil, who came to know JJ in Paris, set his poem “Nightpiece” to music, which was published in The Joyce Book (London: Sylvan Press, 1933). He also planned an electric opera, “Mr. Bloom and the Cyclops” (or “Hero and the Cyclops” [LIII 181]), based on Ulysses, but this never went further than sketches, though an “extract” was printed as a supplement to This Quarter (Milan), vol. 1, no. 2 (Autumn-Winter 1925-1926). The opera was to be scored for sixteen mechanical pianos, eight xylophones controlled from a switchboard, a gramophone playing a recording of a full orchestra, four bass drums, four buzzers, two electric motors, and amplified voice and chorus.

JJ became consumed with the idea that Antheil should write an opera based on Lord Byron’s closet drama Cain: A Mystery (1821), which depicts the story of Cain and Abel from the murderer and outcast Cain’s point of view. JJ wanted Antheil to write the opera for John O’Sullivan, as a vehicle for his “stage presence, diction and voice combined” (LI 292). Antheil preferred that JJ write the libretto, but JJ refused “to rewrite the text of a great English poet,” though he was willing to have someone “curtail the text of the first and third acts” and use JJ’s name for publicity, since he was “quite content to go down to posterity as a scissors and paste man” (LI 297).

To JJ’s disappointment, Antheil wriggled free of the Cain project, possibly as a result of some dissuasion by Pound, or so JJ suspected (LIII 208-09). Pound was indeed unenthusiastic. He wrote JJ a bluntly dismissive note on 9 October 1930: “Am verrry jewbious about G.A. being the composer fer a opry about the 2 jewriginal jew bhoys” (Spoo, “Unpublished Letters of Ezra Pound to James, Nora, and Stanislaus Joyce,” 554). Antheil’s memoir Bad Boy of Music (1945; rpt. New York: Samuel French, 1990) describes his life and career in Paris in the 1920s and his friendships and collaborations with Pound and JJ (117-23, 150-55). (See also Nora Barnacle to Ezra and Dorothy Pound, 25 June 1930, notes.)

div.note: JJ described the accident to Harriet Shaw Weaver: “I was crossing the Esplanade des Invalides [in Paris] about 4 p.m. in a taxi alone and a private car ran into it. I was flung violently forward and then as violently back but escaped any glass in the eye. I had a big bump on my forehead and a bad pain in my back, but the doctor who examined me said there was no internal injury” (LI 294). Pound replied to this news: “Glad to hear the auto accident not catastrophic” (Spoo, “Unpublished Letters of Ezra Pound to James, Nora, and Stanislaus Joyce,” 554).

Since early 1925, Pound and his wife Dorothy, née Shakespear (1886-1973), were living in a top-floor apartment at 12 via Marsala in the Italian coastal town of Rapallo, some fifteen miles from Genoa, with views of the sea and the hills. They remained there for nearly twenty years (see JJ to Pound, 31 December 1924, notes).
